title: What is Liquibase, and how does it manage database schema version control (changeSets, changelogs, databasechangelog)?
shortTitle: What Liquibase is and how it manages database schema version control — changeSets, changelogs, databasechangelog

s1_definition.profdef: Liquibase is an open-source database schema change-management tool that brings version control to the database the same way git brings it to code. You describe every schema change as a changeSet — a uniquely identified, ordered unit of change such as creating a table or adding a column — and you organize changeSets into a changelog file that Liquibase reads in order. When Liquibase runs against a database, it records every applied changeSet in a tracking table called DATABASECHANGELOG, so on the next run it knows exactly which changeSets are already applied and executes only the new ones. This makes schema evolution repeatable, ordered, and identical across every environment, and it supports rollback and safe team collaboration.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a master ledger of every structural change ever made to its record-keeping system: "added a column for UPI reference on this date," "created the loans table on that date." Each entry is numbered and signed, and the bank keeps a checklist of which changes each branch has already carried out. When a new branch opens, staff simply run down the master list in order, skipping anything already done, so every branch ends up with exactly the same structure. Liquibase is that master ledger and checklist for the database schema, and DATABASECHANGELOG is the checklist of what each database has already applied.
s1_definition.oneliner: Liquibase is git for your database schema — ordered changeSets in a changelog, and a DATABASECHANGELOG table that remembers what has already been applied so each environment converges to the same structure safely.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Liquibase is an open-source database schema change-management tool that brings version control to the database the same way git brings it to code. You describe every schema change as a changeSet — a uniquely identified, ordered unit of change such as creating a table or adding a column — and you organize changeSets into a changelog file that Liquibase reads in order. When Liquibase runs against a database, it records every applied changeSet in a tracking table called DATABASECHANGELOG, so on the next run it knows exactly which changeSets are already applied and executes only the new ones. This makes schema evolution repeatable, ordered, and identical across every environment, and it supports rollback and safe team collaboration.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps a master ledger of every structural change ever made to its record-keeping system: "added a column for UPI reference on this date," "created the loans table on that date." Each entry is numbered and signed, and the bank keeps a checklist of which changes each branch has already carried out. When a new branch opens, staff simply run down the master list in order, skipping anything already done, so every branch ends up with exactly the same structure. Liquibase is that master ledger and checklist for the database schema, and DATABASECHANGELOG is the checklist of what each database has already applied.

**One line to remember:** Liquibase is git for your database schema — ordered changeSets in a changelog, and a DATABASECHANGELOG table that remembers what has already been applied so each environment converges to the same structure safely.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem Liquibase solves is that databases drift. Without a tool, one developer runs a CREATE TABLE by hand on their machine, another forgets to apply it to staging, and production ends up subtly different, which in a bank is a serious risk. Application code is versioned in git, but the schema it depends on often is not, so the two fall out of sync. Liquibase makes the schema a versioned, reproducible artifact that travels with the code.

A changeSet is the atomic unit. Each changeSet has three identifying parts: an id, an author, and the file it lives in, and together these form a unique identity. A changeSet contains one logical change, such as creating a table, adding a column, creating an index, or inserting seed data. The golden rule is that a changeSet, once committed and applied anywhere, is immutable — you never edit it afterwards, because other databases have already applied it and editing it would make their recorded state inconsistent. If you need to change something, you add a new changeSet. Liquibase enforces this by storing a checksum of each changeSet; if you alter an already-applied changeSet, the checksum no longer matches and Liquibase refuses to run, warning you of the tampering.

A changelog is the ordered master file that lists changeSets, or includes other changelog files. It can be written in SQL, XML, YAML, or JSON. A common structure is a root changelog that includes one file per release or per feature, so the history reads as a clear, append-only timeline. Because the order is explicit and fixed, running the changelog against an empty database reproduces the exact schema step by step, and running it against an existing database applies only what is missing.

The DATABASECHANGELOG table is how Liquibase tracks state inside the database itself. The first time Liquibase runs, it creates this table automatically. For every changeSet it applies, it inserts a row recording the id, author, filename, the checksum, the execution date, and the order. On subsequent runs, Liquibase reads this table, compares it to the changelog, and executes only changeSets that are not already recorded. This is what makes runs idempotent: you can run the same changelog a hundred times and it will only ever apply each changeSet once. There is a companion table, DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK, which holds a lock so that two application instances starting at the same time do not try to apply migrations simultaneously; one acquires the lock and the other waits.

The typical workflow in a banking microservice is that Liquibase runs automatically at application startup or as a dedicated pipeline step before deployment. The developer adds a new changeSet to the changelog, commits it with the code, and when the service starts in any environment, Liquibase brings that environment's schema up to date by applying exactly the new changeSets. Because the same changelog runs everywhere, development, staging, and production schemas stay identical. Liquibase also supports rollback: a changeSet can declare how to undo itself, or Liquibase can auto-generate rollback for simple changes, so you can revert the last few changeSets if a release goes wrong.

The senior-level nuance connects back to safe deployments. For zero-downtime rolling updates where the old and new application versions run simultaneously, schema changes must be backward compatible during the overlap, which is the expand-and-contract pattern, and Liquibase is the tool that executes each of those steps as separate, ordered changeSets: one release adds the new column, a later release removes the old one. You also use preconditions to make changeSets defensive — for example only add a column if it does not already exist — and you use contexts and labels to run certain changeSets only in certain environments, such as inserting test seed data only in development. And critically, destructive changeSets like dropping a column are reviewed carefully and separated from the release that stops using that column, because in a bank you never drop data that a rollback might still need.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the accounts service needs its schema to evolve safely across many environments and many developers without drift.

Problem 1 — The accounts table must be created once, consistently, everywhere. If each environment were set up by hand, they would diverge. This is exactly what a changeSet in a changelog solves: the create-table change is applied in the same order everywhere.

Problem 2 — Later, a new column for a UPI handle must be added, but only to environments that do not already have it, and without re-running the original create. This is exactly what DATABASECHANGELOG tracking solves: Liquibase applies only the new changeSet because the create-table changeSet is already recorded.

Problem 3 — Two application instances start at once during a rolling deploy and both try to migrate. This is exactly what the DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK solves: only one instance migrates while the other waits.

To make this runnable without a real database, we will build a small program that models Liquibase's engine. It will contain a `ChangeSet` with id, author, forward SQL, and a checksum, a `ChangeLog` holding an ordered list, a `DatabaseChangeLogTable` recording applied changeSets, a `ChangeLogLock` modelling the lock, and a `LiquibaseRunner` that applies only unapplied changeSets and verifies checksums. The demo runs the changelog once to create the table, adds a new changeSet for the UPI column, runs again to show only the new one applies, and attempts to tamper with an applied changeSet to show checksum protection.

Project structure:

```
accounts-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/liquibase/
│   │   │   ├── LiquibaseDemo.java                 (main class)
│   │   │   ├── model/
│   │   │   │   └── ChangeSet.java
│   │   │   ├── changelog/
│   │   │   │   └── ChangeLog.java
│   │   │   ├── tracking/
│   │   │   │   ├── DatabaseChangeLogTable.java      (DATABASECHANGELOG)
│   │   │   │   └── ChangeLogLock.java               (DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK)
│   │   │   └── engine/
│   │   │       └── LiquibaseRunner.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── db/changelog/
│   │           └── db.changelog-master.yaml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/liquibase/
│           └── engine/
│               └── LiquibaseRunnerTest.java
```

The real changelog is part of the deliverable:

```yaml
# src/main/resources/db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml
databaseChangeLog:
  - changeSet:
      id: 1-create-accounts
      author: rajesh
      changes:
        - createTable:
            tableName: accounts
            columns:
              - column: { name: id, type: VARCHAR(20), constraints: { primaryKey: true } }
              - column: { name: holder_name, type: VARCHAR(100) }
              - column: { name: balance, type: DECIMAL(15,2) }
      rollback:
        - dropTable: { tableName: accounts }
  - changeSet:
      id: 2-add-upi-handle
      author: priya
      preConditions:
        - onFail: MARK_RAN
        - not: [ columnExists: { tableName: accounts, columnName: upi_handle } ]
      changes:
        - addColumn:
            tableName: accounts
            columns:
              - column: { name: upi_handle, type: VARCHAR(50) }
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the model
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/accounts-service-1.0.0.jar

# Real Liquibase commands against a database
liquibase --changeLogFile=db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml update
liquibase --changeLogFile=db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml rollbackCount 1
liquibase status   # shows which changeSets are not yet applied
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a changelog starting with one changeSet that creates the accounts table, later gaining a second changeSet that adds a UPI handle column, run against a tracking table that starts empty.

Step 1: On the first run, the runner acquires the changelog lock so no other instance can migrate concurrently. It then reads the changelog, which contains only the create-accounts changeSet.

Step 2: The runner checks the DATABASECHANGELOG tracking table and finds the create-accounts changeSet is not recorded. It applies the forward SQL that creates the table, then records the changeSet's identity and checksum in the tracking table. The lock is released.

Step 3: A second changeSet, add-upi-handle, is appended to the changelog, and the runner is invoked again. It re-acquires the lock and reads both changeSets in order.

Step 4: For the create-accounts changeSet, the runner finds it already recorded in the tracking table and verifies that its stored checksum matches the current one, confirming nobody edited it. Because it is already applied and unchanged, the runner skips it. This is the idempotency that prevents re-creating the table.

Step 5: For the add-upi-handle changeSet, the runner finds it is not yet recorded, so it applies the alter-table forward SQL and records it. Only the new change ran; the environment converged to the latest schema without touching what was already there.

Step 6: To demonstrate protection, the create-accounts changeSet is illegally edited after having been applied. On the next run, the runner computes its checksum, compares it to the stored one, and finds they differ. It throws a checksum-mismatch error and refuses to proceed, exactly as real Liquibase does, because an altered applied changeSet means some databases have a different version of that change and the history is no longer trustworthy.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 3:20:14 AM com.bank.liquibase.LiquibaseDemo main
INFO: === first run (fresh database) ===
INFO: applying: 1-create-accounts::rajesh::master.yaml -> CREATE TABLE accounts (id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, balance DECIMAL(15,2))
INFO: === second run (cs1 already applied) ===
INFO: applying: 2-add-upi-handle::priya::master.yaml -> ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN upi_handle VARCHAR(50)
INFO: === tampering with an applied changeSet ===
SEVERE: Liquibase refused to run: checksum mismatch for 1-create-accounts::rajesh::master.yaml — changeSet was altered!
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  App starts (any environment) → LiquibaseRunner.update(changeLog)
    │
    ▼ acquire DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK (one instance migrates, others wait)
    │
    ▼ read changelog (ordered changeSets)
    │
    ├─ changeSet "1-create-accounts"
    │     in DATABASECHANGELOG?  ── no ──→ apply SQL → record (id, checksum)
    │                            ── yes ─→ checksum match? ── yes → skip
    │                                                      └─ no  → ABORT (tampered)
    │
    ├─ changeSet "2-add-upi-handle"
    │     not recorded ──→ apply ALTER TABLE → record
    │
    ▼ release lock
  Result: every environment converges to the same schema, each change applied once
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Liquibase Engine ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Command/Ledger: each ChangeSet is an applied, recorded command    │
  │     WHY: idempotent re-runs via DATABASECHANGELOG tracking         │
  │  Guarded section: ChangeLogLock serializes concurrent migrations   │
  │     WHY: two instances must not migrate at once                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: ChangeSet=one change, ChangeLog=ordering, Runner=application   │
  │  O: new change = new changeSet; never edit an applied one          │
  │  D: Runner depends on tracking + lock abstractions                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   LiquibaseRunner     │───────▶│  DatabaseChangeLogTable  │
  │ - tracking            │ reads/ │  + isApplied(id)         │
  │ - lock                │ writes │  + storedChecksum(id)    │
  │ + update(changeLog)   │        │  + record(id, checksum)  │
  └──────────┬───────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘
             │ uses                ┌──────────────────────────┐
             ├───────────────────▶ │  ChangeLogLock           │
             │                     │  + acquire() + release() │
             │ iterates            └──────────────────────────┘
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐◆──────▶┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   ChangeLog           │ owns   │  ChangeSet               │
  │ - changeSets: List    │ (1..*) │  + identity()            │
  │ + add(cs)             │        │  + checksum()            │
  └──────────────────────┘        │  + forwardSql/rollbackSql│
                                   └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: changeSet lifecycle ─────────────────────
  [authored] → [committed to changelog] → [applied + recorded] → [immutable]
        (edit after applied → checksum mismatch → run ABORTS)

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. LiquibaseRunner.update(changeLog)
  2.   → ChangeLogLock.acquire()
  3.   → for each ChangeSet: tracking.isApplied(identity)?
  4.       → no → apply forwardSql → tracking.record(id, checksum)
  5.       → yes → checksum match? skip : ABORT
  6.   → ChangeLogLock.release()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Liquibase is a database schema change-management tool that brings version control to the database the same way git does to code. I describe every schema change as a changeSet, which is the atomic unit of change — create a table, add a column, create an index. Each changeSet is identified by its id, its author, and the file it lives in, and together those form a unique identity. The golden rule is that once a changeSet has been committed and applied anywhere, it is immutable: I never edit it, because other databases have already applied it; instead I add a new changeSet. Liquibase enforces this by storing a checksum of each changeSet, so if anyone alters an applied changeSet the checksum no longer matches and Liquibase refuses to run.

ChangeSets live in a changelog, which is the ordered master file, often a root file that includes one changelog per release so the history reads as a clean append-only timeline. Because the order is explicit and fixed, running the changelog against an empty database rebuilds the exact schema step by step, and running it against an existing database applies only what is missing. The way Liquibase knows what is missing is the DATABASECHANGELOG table, which it creates automatically inside the database and into which it writes a row for every changeSet it applies, recording the id, author, filename, checksum, and date. On each run it reads that table, compares it to the changelog, and executes only the changeSets not already recorded, which makes runs idempotent — I can run the same changelog any number of times and each change applies exactly once. A companion DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK table holds a lock so two instances starting together do not migrate simultaneously; one migrates while the other waits.

In a banking microservice I run Liquibase either at application startup or as a dedicated pipeline step before deployment. A developer adds a changeSet, commits it with the code, and when the service starts in any environment Liquibase brings that environment's schema up to date, so development, staging, and production stay identical and never drift. Liquibase also supports rollback, where a changeSet declares how to undo itself or Liquibase generates it for simple changes, so I can revert the last few changeSets if a release goes wrong.

The nuance I always raise is how this ties to safe, zero-downtime deployments. When old and new application versions run together during a rolling update, schema changes must stay backward compatible through the overlap, which is the expand-and-contract pattern, and Liquibase executes each step as a separate ordered changeSet — one release adds the new column, a later release removes the old one. At National Bank of India I used preconditions so a changeSet only adds a column if it does not already exist, contexts so test seed data runs only in development, and I kept destructive changes like dropping a column carefully separated from the release that stopped using it, because in a bank you never drop data a rollback might still need. That discipline is what made our schema a trustworthy, versioned, auditable artifact rather than a source of production surprises.
